title: The Weight
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of isolation and unspoken grief
excerpt: He was gaining weight. Six kilos in a Tuesday morning. The scale was not broken. He was not fatter. He was Thomas Doran and something else, and the something else had by Friday a mass of twelve kilos, and it was gaining mass at approximately one kilo per hour, and it was inside him.

chapters.title: The Scale
chapters.body:
He was gaining weight.

Thomas Doran was fifty-four years old, and he had for the last two decades weighed, with a variance of no more than a kilogram in either direction, exactly seventy-eight kilos. He had weighed seventy-eight kilos through his divorce. He had weighed seventy-eight kilos through the long slow decline and death of his father. He had weighed seventy-eight kilos through the year he had, on the advice of a doctor he did not entirely trust, tried to gain muscle by drinking protein shakes in the morning, and he had weighed seventy-eight kilos through the subsequent year he had, on the advice of a different doctor, given up the protein shakes. He was seventy-eight kilos. He had made his peace with it.

He stepped on the bathroom scale one Tuesday morning in October, in the small ritual he had performed every Tuesday and Friday morning since he was thirty, and the scale said eighty-four.

He stared at the number.

He stepped off the scale. He stepped on again. He tried to hold his weight evenly. He watched the digital display flicker, settle, produce, after a moment's thought, the same number.

Eighty-four kilos.

He was not, he knew instantly, six kilos heavier than he had been the previous Friday. He would have known. His trousers still fit. His belt was on the same notch. His face in the mirror was the same face. He had eaten no more than he usually ate, and he had walked, as he usually walked, twenty minutes to and from the tram stop every day, and he had slept, as he usually slept, six and a half hours per night.

He stepped off the scale. He waited. He stepped on again.

Eighty-four point one.

He stared at the display. He counted, silently, in his head, up to twenty. He watched the display, patient, waiting for it to change.

The number climbed by another decimal.

Eighty-four point two.

He stepped off the scale, and stayed off, and stood on the cold tiles of his bathroom floor in his boxer shorts, and thought about what he had just seen.

The scale, he told himself, was broken. Scales broke. Digital scales especially broke — the load cells inside them wore out and produced spurious readings, and the correct response was to buy a new scale, or to have the old one recalibrated, and not to stand in one's own bathroom at six-thirty in the morning terrifying oneself with a machine that had been made in China for the equivalent of eight pounds.

He put on his clothes. He went to work.

He did not think about the scale during the day. He thought about the two reports on his desk, and the meeting at eleven, and the client in Frankfurt who had been unreasonable about the delivery schedule and would be more unreasonable now, and his sister's birthday, which was on Saturday, and about which he would need to remember to send a card. He was, in general, a man who did not think about scales during the day. He had not become the kind of man who did.

He thought about it, however, that evening.

He thought about it while making his dinner, which was, as it had been on Tuesday evenings for eleven years, salmon and rice and one of the two vegetables that were in the refrigerator. He thought about it while eating. He thought about it while washing his single plate. And when he had finished his tea and had turned off the kitchen light and had gone into the bathroom to brush his teeth, he thought, as one thinks these thoughts, that he might as well settle the matter.

He stood on the scale in his pyjamas.

Eighty-four point four.

He looked at the number for a long time.

He got off the scale. He looked at himself in the mirror. He was not, he told himself, six and a half kilos heavier than he had been on Friday. He looked at his stomach. He turned sideways and looked at his stomach. He pressed his stomach with his hand. He was not fatter. He was not swollen. He was not, in any visible way, larger.

He got on the scale again.

Eighty-four point five.

He got off. He got on. He watched the number.

It did not go down.

—

He bought a new scale on Wednesday.

He bought it at the department store on his lunch break, a mechanical one this time, no batteries, no load cells, just a spring and a dial. He carried it home in a paper bag on the tram, and he set it up in the bathroom, and he stepped on it in his boxer shorts, and it said, after settling, eighty-five kilos exactly.

He got off the scale.

He looked at the old scale, which he had not thrown away. He put the old scale next to the new one. He stepped on the old one.

Eighty-five point one.

He stepped off the old one and onto the new one.

Eighty-five point two.

He stood on the tile floor between the two scales. He was breathing shallowly. He had begun, at some point in the last minute, to breathe shallowly, and he made himself take a full breath, and then another, and he thought carefully.

The scales agreed.

Both scales were saying the same thing. Both scales had, since Tuesday morning, added another kilo to whatever it was they were telling him, and were continuing to add small amounts, in real time, as he stood on them.

The scales, he understood, were not broken.

He walked back into the bedroom. He sat on the edge of the bed. He put his hands on his knees. He looked at his hands.

His hands looked the same. They looked like the hands of a fifty-four-year-old man who worked in logistics for a mid-sized shipping firm, who had a small flat on the third floor of a converted warehouse in the older part of the city, who had not been married for eight years and did not, on the whole, expect to be married again. His hands were his hands. They were, if anything, thinner than they had been ten years ago, because everyone's hands got a little thinner as they got older, as the small muscles between the bones subsided.

He was gaining weight. But he was not gaining any part of himself that he could see.

He said, aloud, in his empty bedroom: *what.*

The word came out as a question and stayed as a question. There was no answer, of course. There was, in his flat at ten p.m. on a Wednesday, no one to answer.

He stood up. He went back into the bathroom. He got on the new scale.

Eighty-six.

He got off.

He did not sleep well.

—

By Friday morning he was ninety kilos.

He had gained, in three days, twelve kilos. He was gaining, by his rough calculation, four kilos a day, and the rate was, if anything, accelerating. He had checked, on Thursday evening, by weighing himself once every hour for four hours before bed, and the rate had gone from three and a half kilos in the first three hours to just over one and a half kilos in the last hour alone.

He was not larger. He was not, in the mirror, in any way changed. He had put on his trousers on Friday morning and they had fit exactly as they had on Tuesday. His belt was on the same notch. His shirt buttoned normally. If a stranger had passed him on the street, they would not have looked at him twice. He was a middle-aged man in a grey coat with a briefcase. He was Thomas Doran.

He was Thomas Doran and something else. He did not yet know what the something else was, but it had, by Friday morning, a mass of just over twelve kilos, and it was gaining mass at approximately one kilo per hour, and it was inside him.

He did not go to work on Friday.

He sent a message to his supervisor saying he was ill. This was, in a way, true. He was ill in the sense that something was very wrong. He was not ill in the sense that would satisfy the office, but the office did not need to know that.

He sat in his flat with the two scales side by side on the bathroom tile, and he watched himself gain weight.

He watched for an hour. His weight went from ninety point three to ninety-one point five. He watched, in that hour, the numbers change in real time, on the digital scale, at intervals of ten to twenty minutes, small clicks upward that he could see if he stood very still.

He got off the scale.

He walked into his kitchen. He drank a glass of water. He looked out the small window over the sink, at the alley between his building and the next, where a black cat was picking its way delicately along the top of a wall.

He thought about his father.

His father had died at sixty-seven of what the doctors had called complications, which had turned out on the death certificate to be pancreatic cancer, which had by the time of the diagnosis been at stage four and inoperable, and which had killed his father over four months of steadily decreasing weight and steadily increasing pain. His father had, at the end, weighed forty-three kilos. Thomas remembered his father's hand on the hospital bedsheet, thin and blue-veined and light, and he remembered the small dry weight of his father's hand when he had picked it up.

Thomas thought: *this is not that.*

He thought: *whatever this is, it is not that.*

He knew this because whatever was gaining mass inside him was not gaining it *at his expense*. His hands were not thinning. His face was not sunken. He was not tired in the specific hungry tired way of a man whose body was being eaten. He felt, in fact, fine. He felt slightly hungry, because it was noon and he had not eaten breakfast, but he felt otherwise entirely well. He was Thomas Doran, walking around in a body that weighed, at this precise moment, ninety-one point seven kilos and rising, and he felt exactly as he had felt on Monday.

He was not, he understood, dying.

He was being *added to.*

—

He sat down in the small armchair in the corner of his living room, and he tried to work out what to do.

He thought about going to a hospital. He rehearsed, in his mind, the conversation. *Doctor, I've gained twelve kilos in three days.* *Have you been eating more?* *No.* *Are you retaining fluid? Are your feet swollen? Your face?* *No.* *Then are you sure you've gained the weight?* *Yes, doctor. I have two scales. They agree.*

He imagined the doctor's expression.

He imagined being sent for tests. He imagined an MRI machine. He imagined the technicians looking at the scan afterward with expressions of professional patience. He imagined a specialist. He imagined being kept in the hospital overnight, and then for several nights, and then for a week, while the specialists did further tests and produced further theories and, eventually, admitted that they did not know what he had.

He imagined the possibility, more likely than not, that once they had done enough tests, they would want to open him up.

He sat in the armchair and he thought about being opened up.

He did not want to be opened up.

He did not know why, precisely, he did not want this. He was a rational man. He had lived a rational life. He believed in medicine and in doctors and in the small correct machinery of modern healthcare, and if any of his friends had come to him with a story like his own he would have said, without hesitation, *go to a hospital.*

But he did not want to be opened up.

He sat with this feeling for a long time, and eventually he was able to name it. It was not exactly fear. It was more like a *reluctance* — a resistance in his chest, a small settled objection, as if some part of him that he did not usually consult had already been consulted and had produced a firm answer.

The part of him that had produced the answer was, he understood after some further sitting, the part of him that was, at this moment, weighing twelve extra kilos.

Whatever was inside him did not want to be opened up.

Thomas Doran sat in his armchair on a Friday afternoon in October and understood, with a clarity he had not asked for, that he was in the presence of something that had a preference.

He got up. He went into the bathroom. He looked at the scale.

Ninety-three kilos.

He got on. He watched the number climb, slowly and patiently, from ninety-three to ninety-three point one. He watched it for a full minute. He watched it click, at the end of the minute, to ninety-three point two.

He said, aloud, to the scale, to the something inside him, to whatever there was to hear:

*What are you.*

The scale did not answer.

Nothing answered.

Thomas Doran stood on the scale in his bathroom, in his pyjamas, on a Friday afternoon in October, and waited for whatever was inside him to make the next move.

chapters.title: The Room in Him
chapters.body:
By Sunday he had figured out that it moved.

He had discovered this by lying still.

He had, on Saturday, weighed himself twenty-three times over the course of the day, and had watched the number climb from ninety-six kilos in the morning to one hundred and eight by evening, and had understood, from the sheer speed of it, that whatever was inside him was still growing, and would continue to grow, and that at the current rate he would, within a week, weigh more than any human body was engineered to carry.

He had not eaten much that day. He had not been hungry. He had drunk water because he was thirsty, and he had eaten a piece of toast because he had felt he should, and by evening he had begun to be aware of a low, faint pressure in his chest — not a pain, not a discomfort, but a *presence*, a sense that something in the small space beneath his sternum was more definite than it had been.

He had lain down on his bed to think.

He had been lying still on his back, staring at the ceiling, for perhaps ten minutes when he had felt it.

A small internal shift. A weight moving inside him. Not a fluttering, not a peristalsis, not any sensation he had had before in his own body. It had been the sensation of an object of some mass — a small heavy object, perhaps the size of an orange — turning slowly against the inside of his ribs.

He had held his breath.

He had waited.

The weight had shifted again. This time he had felt it distinctly enough to trace, in his mind, the path of it. It had moved from a place near his heart, on his left side, to a place lower down and toward his right — a slow patient displacement, taking perhaps thirty seconds, ending with a small settled *tuck*, as if the object had found a new resting position and was now, once again, still.

Thomas had lain on his bed for a long time not moving.

He had thought, very clearly: *there is something in me.*

He had thought: *it moves.*

He had thought, and this thought had come to him with a strange calm: *it is aware that I am lying down.*

He had not known, when he had thought this, how he knew. He had known, however, that he did.

—

On Sunday morning he weighed one hundred and fifteen kilos.

He got on the scale in his pyjamas, and the number came up, and he stood there and looked at it. He did not, this time, feel any particular alarm. He had, over the course of Saturday, moved past alarm and into some quieter place. He had understood that whatever was happening to him was going to continue happening, and that his ordinary emotional responses — the alarm, the disbelief, the impulse to call someone — were not going to change the situation, and were therefore, in a practical sense, not worth expending. He had put them away.

He was, he understood, in a different state now.

He had entered, he thought, the state one entered when something very large began to happen to one's life and continued happening for long enough that one adjusted. It was the state he had been in, twenty-two years ago, when his marriage had ended and he had understood that the ending was going to take several more months of formal proceedings and that he could either spend those months in fresh grief every morning or in a kind of settled attention, and had chosen the second. It was the state he had been in when his father had begun to die and Thomas had understood that the dying was going to take four months, and that he was going to have to be present for each of those four months without letting the anticipatory grief of the end colour every day of the middle, and had, mostly, managed it.

It was, he understood, the state of someone who had accepted the shape of what was happening and had decided to be interested in it instead of afraid of it.

He was interested. He had, he realized, been interested since Wednesday.

He had, on some level below thinking, been *waiting* to be interested in something for a very long time.

—

By Sunday afternoon he had begun to test it.

He had begun, cautiously, to see what the thing inside him would do.

He had lain on the bed, and he had lifted his left arm slowly into the air, and he had felt, after a delay of perhaps three seconds, the weight inside him shift toward his left side — not lift, not roll, but *adjust*, as if the object had noted the change in the balance of the body it was inside and had moved to compensate. He had lowered his arm. The weight had shifted back.

He had turned onto his right side. The weight had shifted, again with a small delay, toward his right — and had settled there, in the space between his ribs and his hip, in a position it had not, so far, occupied when he was sitting or standing.

He had turned onto his left side. The weight had crossed his body, slowly, taking perhaps a full minute, and had settled again in the equivalent position on his left.

He had sat up. The weight had risen slowly through his chest and had come to rest, once more, in the small space beneath his sternum.

He had understood, then, several things at once.

He had understood that the thing inside him had *shape*. It was not a fluid, not a mass, not a tumor. It was a body. It had, at each shift, moved as a body would move — an object of definite size and mass and volume, adjusting itself with intent to occupy the position most comfortable for whatever it was.

He had understood that it was, at present, smaller than he was. It was not filling his abdomen. It was, in fact, contained, in the position it currently occupied, in a space roughly the size of his own two hands. It had substantial mass — thirty-seven extra kilos, by that afternoon's weight — but it did not, apparently, take up the volume that thirty-seven kilos of ordinary flesh would take. It was denser than flesh. Very much denser.

He had understood that whatever it was, it was resting.

He had understood, further, that it was resting because he was lying down. It had settled the way a passenger might settle in a chair when a train stopped. It was waiting.

He had sat up. He had waited for the weight to rise into his chest, and for the small tuck of settlement to signal that it had, once more, arranged itself.

He had said, out loud, in his bedroom: *can you hear me.*

He had not expected an answer. He had not, particularly, been asking for one. He had been asking because the situation seemed to call for it, because when one was in the presence of something one wished to understand, one asked.

The thing inside him had not spoken.

But it had done something else.

It had, three seconds after his question, shifted its position by a fraction. A small definite movement, no more than a settling. But it had happened *in response* to his voice — at the precise interval, three seconds, at which every other movement had happened in response to a change he had made in his body. It had responded.

Thomas Doran had sat on the edge of his bed on a Sunday afternoon in October, at one hundred and eighteen kilos, and had understood that there was, inside his body, something that was listening.

—

He had spent the rest of Sunday learning what it would do.

He did not, at any point, name it. He was aware that if he had begun to name it — *the thing*, *the guest*, *the passenger* — he would have made it, in his own mind, a companion, and he was not yet prepared to have a companion inside himself. He kept his mind on it as *what was there*. What was there. What was there when he leaned forward and pressed his palm against his sternum. What was there when he lay flat and it settled. What was there when he spoke.

He had learned that it responded to two things.

The first was the shape of his body. Any movement he made — sitting, standing, turning, lying down — was met, with a delay of three seconds, by a corresponding shift of what was there. It was, he understood, adjusting itself to remain in whatever position was most comfortable to it, given the position of the body it was inside. It was, as far as he could tell, entirely reactive on this dimension.

The second was his voice.

He had discovered this by accident. He had, on Sunday evening, been talking to himself — quietly, matter-of-factly, describing to himself the situation, in the way he had begun to describe situations to himself since he had begun to live alone — and had noticed that when he spoke, the thing inside him would shift. Not always. Not with every word. But often enough that he began to test it.

He said, aloud: *hello.*

Three seconds. A small shift.

He said, aloud, *are you there.*

Three seconds. A larger shift.

He said, softly: *what do you want.*

Three seconds.

Nothing.

He said, louder: *what do you want.*

Three seconds. A very small shift. Barely perceptible.

He said the same words, softly, again: *what do you want.*

Three seconds. Nothing.

He tried different words. He said his own name. He got a shift. He said his father's name. He got a larger shift. He said his sister's name. He got a shift. He said the names of every person he could think of that he had ever known well, and he got a shift for each of them, of varying sizes, in no pattern that he could immediately discern.

He was in the middle of this experiment, at eleven at night, on a bathroom floor at one hundred and twenty-one kilos, when he said, without meaning to, his ex-wife's name — the name he had not said aloud in the seven years since the divorce papers had been signed, the name he had trained himself, over long careful months, not to think about — and he felt, inside him, the largest shift of the evening. A definite roll of the weight, a movement toward his upper chest, and a settling in a position it had not, before that moment, occupied.

He sat on the bathroom floor and thought about this for a long time.

He said the name again.

The thing inside him did not move a second time. It stayed where it had gone. As if it had reached a position it was, now, content with, and did not need to move again.

He thought: *it likes that name.*

He thought: *it responds to what I care about.*

He thought, and this thought settled in him with the weight of an understanding he had been slowly assembling for days: *it is being fed by what I feel.*

He sat on the bathroom floor and considered this.

He considered the fact that in the seven years since the divorce, he had made a small careful life in which he had rearranged everything he could rearrange so as not to feel very much of anything. He had, over those years, become fluent in the specific work of not-feeling. He had made his flat neat. He had made his job dull. He had made his weekly routines predictable enough that no day required much of him. He had, in short, folded down the emotional life he had once had and put it away in a small compartment, and had let the compartment go quiet.

And then, evidently, something had noticed. Something had come. Something was, now, sitting inside his ribs and eating what he had been storing.

Thomas Doran sat on his bathroom floor and understood, with a small clarity, that whatever was in him was there because he had *let* it.

He had spent seven years building a house that no one lived in.

Something had, at last, moved in.

chapters.title: The Bearing
chapters.body:
He stopped weighing himself on the tenth day.

The scale, by that point, had stopped being useful. The mechanical scale had reached its upper limit of one hundred and twenty kilos on the eighth day and had simply refused to register further, its dial pinned to the last mark. The digital scale had gone on for another day, giving him one hundred and thirty-one, one hundred and thirty-eight, one hundred and forty-two, and then had abruptly returned an error message on Wednesday morning and thereafter refused to display anything but a small blinking rectangle.

Thomas Doran, on the morning of the tenth day, weighed as much as two men. He knew this not because a scale had told him so but because he could no longer stand up from a chair without pushing off with both arms, and because when he lay on his bed the springs of the bed frame groaned in a way they had not previously done, and because, when he had gone to the bathroom on the ninth night and had sat on the toilet, the porcelain had made a soft settling sound he had not heard before, of ceramic under strain.

He was not fatter. He was not swollen. His clothes still fit. His hands were still his hands, his face was still his face, and if a friend had passed him in the street they would not have known.

But he weighed, he thought, perhaps a hundred and eighty kilos. Perhaps more. The rate of increase had slowed since Sunday — the thing inside him had, he thought, grown to some size and was now expanding more slowly, or was gathering mass more efficiently, or had simply reached the point in its development at which growth was no longer the primary activity. He did not know which. He knew only that the increase had slowed from four kilos a day to perhaps one, and that this had been going on for some days, and that he was, now, very heavy.

He had, over the course of the last week, arranged things.

He had cancelled everything he could cancel. He had told his supervisor that he was ill in a way that would require an extended leave, and had produced, without doctor's note, a plausible enough set of symptoms to be granted six weeks of unpaid time. He had told his sister that he was ill, in a different and vaguer way, and had told her not to visit. He had told his mother, in the smallest possible way, that he was unwell but that he was managing, and had refused, gently and with the specific quiet firmness that had always worked with her, to explain further.

He had arranged, through the small grocery shop on his corner, for a weekly delivery of the food he needed. He had told the boy who brought it that Thomas was recovering from surgery and would prefer to leave the money outside the door in an envelope. The boy, who was seventeen and understood boundaries, had nodded and had never asked.

He had, in short, made his flat a place he could be inside without being seen.

He had begun to talk to the thing.

He had not decided to. He had simply, at some point around day six, found himself doing it. He would be sitting in the armchair, or standing at the sink, or lying on the bed, and he would say, aloud, whatever was on his mind. He would say his thoughts about work, and about his sister, and about the small childhood memory he had had that morning of his father's hand on the back of his neck at a station platform when he was six. He would say things, and the thing inside him would shift, or would not shift, in response.

He had learned, over the days, to read the shifts.

A small shift meant it had noticed. A larger shift meant it had noticed and had cared. A very large shift — the sort that had happened when he said his ex-wife's name — meant that it had cared and had, in some sense, *taken something in*.

He had understood, by day eight, that the taking-in was the point.

He had understood that whatever was inside him was, in some way he could not entirely name, a *receiver*. It was there to receive. It was there to hold what he had spent seven years — perhaps a lifetime — not holding. The grief of the divorce. The grief of his father. The grief of the small careful boy he had been at six on the station platform, who had not, at that platform or after, ever been permitted to be held by his father in exactly the way he had needed. The whole slow accumulation of his life, sorted and filed and put away and never dwelt on.

The thing inside him was dwelling on it. In his place.

He had, on the ninth night, said aloud in his bedroom: *is this what you are for.*

The thing had shifted.

He had said, softly: *did I ask for you.*

The thing had not shifted, then. It had stayed exactly where it was.

He had thought about this for some time. He had thought about the shape of the answer that would have been *yes* and the shape of the answer that would have been *no*, and about which was represented by stillness. He had decided, in the end, that stillness meant only that the thing did not have an answer to that question — that the question was, from its position, not applicable. He had not asked for it. He had also not not asked for it. He had spent his life folding down what he could not carry, and the folded thing had, at some threshold he could not identify, become heavy enough that something outside him had come to help him carry it.

He had not asked. And yet, having asked or not, he had produced the necessary weight.

—

On the eleventh day the thing began to speak.

He was sitting in his armchair. He had spent the morning reading, slowly, a book he had bought many years ago and never finished — a slim volume of essays by an English writer who was now dead, about certain small pleasures of solitude, about the quiet lives of the unmarried, about the particular gravity of an empty room at four in the afternoon. He had been reading for perhaps two hours, and had stopped occasionally to think, and to say aloud, to the thing, whatever thoughts arose.

He had said, at one point, something about his mother.

He had said it without particular emotion. It was a small observation about how his mother, at eighty-one, had begun to repeat certain stories from her own childhood, and how these stories were coming back to her in her old age with a specificity they had not, in his memory, had before. He had noted that she had, on the last phone call, told him about the small brown dog she had had as a girl, whose name she had not spoken in decades. He had said, aloud, in his armchair: *she is going back.*

The thing inside him had shifted.

And then, several seconds later, it had spoken.

The word was not spoken in his ear. It was not spoken in the room. It was spoken, if that was the word, *in* him — in the small quiet chamber under his sternum where the thing lay, and where his own thoughts sometimes arose. It was as if a thought had formed there that was not his.

The word was: *yes.*

He had gone very still.

He had waited.

He had said, softly, aloud: *did you say that.*

There was a pause. Then, again, from the same interior chamber:

*Yes.*

—

He did not, at first, know what to do.

He was aware that a rational man in his position would have panicked. He was aware that many people, upon hearing a word spoken inside their own chest by a thing that had been growing inside them for eleven days, would have called for help. He was aware, further, that even a man who had accepted a good deal in the last eleven days — the initial weighing, the discovery of movement, the slow understanding of the thing's purpose — might reasonably draw the line at the thing being *articulate*.

He had drawn no line. He had, after the initial stillness, felt only a slow curious warmth. He had been carrying, without knowing, a companion. And the companion had, at last, and belatedly, decided that it was time to speak.

He had said, aloud, in his empty flat, to the thing beneath his ribs: *how long have you been able to.*

The reply came after the usual three seconds. It was not a word this time but something more like an *impression* — a sense that he had asked a question whose framing was slightly off. The impression carried, in it, something like: *always.*

He had understood then that the thing had been able to speak for the whole of the eleven days he had been listening. It had chosen, until this morning, not to.

He had asked, aloud: *why now.*

The reply had come, again, as an impression, but this one he could translate more easily. It was something like: *you were ready.*

He had sat in his armchair for a long time.

He had eventually said, aloud: *what happens now.*

The thing had, this time, taken longer to answer. It had considered. He could feel it, in a way he could not have described, considering.

At last it had said, in his chest, in that voice that was not exactly a voice:

*I stay.*

*You carry me.*

—

He had thought about this all afternoon.

He had thought about it while he made his tea. He had thought about it while he ate his small dinner of soup and toast. He had thought about it while he stood at the sink washing his cup, and while he brushed his teeth, and while he changed into his pyjamas. He had thought about it, mostly, without emotion, because he had, over the last eleven days, drained most of his emotion into the thing that would carry it.

He had understood, over the course of the afternoon, several things.

He had understood that the arrangement was, in a certain light, a great generosity. He had been carrying the weight of his own unmet life for fifty-four years, alone, and had not known he was doing it, and had not asked to be relieved of it, and the thing had come anyway and had taken the weight into itself and would, from now on, share it. He would be, forever after, a man who weighed twice what a man should weigh. He would move more slowly. He would need to arrange his life carefully. He would not, in all likelihood, be able to leave his flat much. But he would not, ever again, be carrying his life alone.

He had understood that the arrangement was, in another light, a kind of surrender. He had made himself, over the last week, unavailable to his family, to his employer, to the world. He had done so under the guise of illness, but the truth was that he had been withdrawing not from the world's demands but into a private communion with something that had chosen him. He was becoming, day by day, a man who lived inside a small flat with a small companion, and who spoke to it, and who was answered by it, and who was, in every meaningful sense, no longer part of the world he had come from.

He had understood, finally, that he did not particularly mind.

He had understood this last thing with a small quiet clarity, sitting on the edge of his bed on the eleventh night, at whatever weight he was, holding his own hands in his lap. He did not mind. He had never asked for the life he had. He had never asked for the marriage, which had been a mistake. He had never asked for the job, which he had taken because he had had no better idea. He had never asked for the small careful flat, or the small careful routines, or the small careful loneliness. He had accumulated these things because they had happened to him, one by one, and he had not resisted their happening.

The thing inside him had happened to him too. It had, at least, happened *for* a reason. It had happened because he had, without knowing, been asking for it.

He had lain down on the bed. The thing inside him had shifted. He had felt it come to rest against his upper chest, in the position it now preferred at night, the position of a hand laid over a heart.

He had said, softly, into the dark: *what should I call you.*

There had been a long pause.

Then the answer had come, from within him, in the not-voice, quiet and definite:

*Nothing.*

*I am what you did not say.*

—

Thomas Doran was not seen again in the ordinary way.

His sister came to the flat on a Saturday in November, when she had not been able to reach him by telephone for three weeks, and knocked, and got no answer, and eventually, because she was a practical woman and had a spare key, let herself in. The flat was tidy. The kitchen was clean. The bed was made. On the small table beside the armchair was a book of essays with a bookmark three-quarters of the way through, and on the arm of the chair was a folded piece of paper on which her brother had written, in his careful hand: *I am well. Do not look for me. Please tell mother I am well. — Thomas.*

She looked for him. Of course she looked. She reported his disappearance to the police, and the flat was searched, and there was no body, and no signs of struggle, and no clothes missing, and no bank withdrawals, and no sightings, and, in the end, no further information at all.

But if anyone had, in the weeks and months that followed, thought to walk very slowly past the small third-floor window of the flat, with the curtains drawn, they might have heard, some evenings, a quiet voice speaking. And if they had listened, they might have heard, occasionally, an answer.

The voice went on speaking for a long time.

It has not, so far as anyone knows, ever stopped.
